heading: 1 Education of a Meiji Samurai
title_zh: 第一章　一個明治武士的教育
src: At the sound of the noon whistle on 12 October 1903, the clatter of construction suddenly ceased. The workers at the Yokosuka naval shipyard, along the coast to the east of Yokohama, put down their tools and relaxed over their lunches. One of them, thoughtful and little inclined toward the company of his mates, found a place by himself on the deck of the ship where he worked. Once settled, he cautiously opened the newspaper that held his lunch and spread it out before him. It was the staunchly liberal and extremely popular Yorozu Chôhô; the young man who had thus contrived to provide himself with it as noontime reading thought that its outspoken opinions would not agree with those of his fellows. As his eyes passed over the headlines, it suddenly seemed as if “fireworks had struck” them.

The front page announced that his three favourite columnists had resigned. Letters from them explained this decision. They could not, they said, agree with the Yorozu’s decision to concur with the belligerent policy of the government toward Russia. Everyone expected that war would break out shortly.

The young worker was named Arahata Kanson, and almost six decades later he remembered this moment as the turning point in his life. Moved to action by what he read, he went on to become one of the pioneers in the Japanese socialist movement. Many others appear to have been affected one way or another by these notices in the Yorozu. The event stands as one of the turning points in modern Japanese intellectual history.

The three columnists were Kôtoku Denjirô (Shûsui), Sakai Toshihiko (Karekawa), and Uchimura Kanzô. Their frequent articles had contributed an air of impassioned dignity to the Yorozu. Together with the more sensational material on later pages, they had helped to gain it one of the largest circulations in Japan. It suffered in many ways from their departure.

A clear-cut issue had motivated their action. Amid the increasing hysteria that would lead to war, they had all decided to oppose war. The owner of the Yorozu, though himself in agreement with other particulars of their liberal creed, appears to have thought that he could not come out against the government position on such an issue. His columnists chose to resign rather than recant. Their act is rightly remembered for the courage that it required.

Although this was not immediately apparent, the act also foreshadowed a parting of the ways among Japanese influenced by Christianity. Until this time, the columnists had led both those interested in the reform of society and those interested in the problems of personal faith. Now Kôtoku and Sakai turned away from Christianity to lead the socialist movement. Kôtoku died on the scaffold less than ten years later. He had been convicted, though without much evidence, of a plot to assassinate the emperor. Sakai, later to be joined by Arahata, continued his attempts to arouse interest in socialism against increasingly effective government opposition.

Uchimura had worked with Kôtoku and Sakai on their social reform schemes while their desks stood together in the Yorozu offices. After his resignation, Uchimura ceased his attempts to change society and concentrated instead on individual reform. He hoped that those for whom he wrote and whom he counselled would themselves in time become the instruments of social improvement. In the meantime, he remained apart from those who argued that economic disparity made revolution inevitable. “No ‘socialists,’” he crisply requested when suggesting to a friend that they meet for lunch. Those impatient for quick change in society would have to look elsewhere than to Uchimura, even though they had found his writings congenial in the past.

Although his act at this time has earned him a place in Japanese history, its meaning for the society at large is not so much of concern here as its significance for Uchimura. Here in the full power of his professional life he consciously and confidently pens a note that he knows will probably cut him off from a good job and a steady income. His short letter begins, “It is my conviction that war with Russia will mean the destruction of Japan.” Once the people have decided on such a war, he will not “have the heart” to oppose it, yet as a commentator on public affairs, if he does not set forth his convictions, he will discredit his profession. Therefore, he has decided to retire temporarily from the world of social commentary.

Uchimura was in his early forties. Born into a responsible samurai family, he had observed close up some of the action in the War of the Restoration and realized for the rest of his life the profound impact on him that the Restoration had brought. Later, trained to act as a buffer between Japan and the menacing Western powers, he had become a Christian, studied in the United States, and then made national headlines with his hesitation to accord proper respect to a statement that later Americans might have compared to their own Pledge of Allegiance. His temerity had cost him his prestigious government position and forced him to fashion a much less secure life as a writer. His present position as chief editor of the Yorozu had come his way because of his ability at trenchant criticism of the establishment. Large numbers of readers admired his clearly stated opinions. He would move on from this position as a leading opinion maker to a second career far removed from the centres of economic and political power. Looking back, Uchimura realized that as a boy he had been a “fretful timid child,” and this timidity seems to have been directly related to the conditions that affected his family as he grew up. Three personality traits reappear in Kanzô as an adolescent and young man. They form a triangle of forces like those of a vector diagram. At one moment one predominates, at another moment one of the others is stronger, yet all three continue as important in his personality equation. The three are a desire for affection, an oppressive sense of responsibility, and a need to dominate his surroundings. The last trait expresses itself in two ways: at times through a kind of undifferentiated fear and at other times through an overweening ambition.

The ambition seems to exist to enable Kanzô to overcome the fear; he hopes that with continued success he will feel strong and confident. He tries, therefore, to delimit his world and to dominate it like a pioneer in a clearing who must remain vigilant lest the surrounding verdure and its creatures consume him.

Many men share these personality characteristics, but Kanzô exhibited them to an uncommon degree and for an uncommon length of time. No one can say whence this particular constellation of traits came; it may have been partially hereditary, but it is reasonable to suppose that the society in which he grew up, his family, and his schools had considerable influence. I will deal first with his family and then with his education.

The great event in Kanzô’s boyhood was the complex of changes that realigned the forces within Japanese society after the “restoration” of the emperor to power in 1868. The term refers to the centralization of authority under a national government after many generations of dispersed authority. Historians rightly argue whether this event is in fact as pivotal to an understanding of history as it has seemed. Whether it is or not, to many individuals who experienced it, the changes seemed to comprise the most important event of their lives. Those who had belonged to the privileged classes under the old order lamented the end of an agreeable and accustomed way of life. Just as the event seemed crucial, so too the cause of that event seemed clear; it was the impingement of the various Western nations upon the shorelines of Japan. The movement to centralize political power developed as a reaction to this threat against Japan’s sovereignty, and the new Restoration government ultimately kept Japan free in the face of Western expansion. Patriotic Japanese could not therefore consider the Restoration as other than good, no matter how it affected their own lives. They might have felt greatly aggrieved by it, but they could in conscience direct any consequent hostilities only at the source of the trouble that had brought on the Restoration: the foreigners, who had started it all.

A short civil war followed the declaration by the Imperial party that it intended to restore power to the emperor, the move that symbolized its new nationalization. Troops of both sides, one group hot upon the heels of the other, passed near Kanzô’s family home within a few months of his seventh birthday. It is therefore probable that Kanzô could later recall the sense of contingency that accompanied the greatest event of his childhood. Much as those born in the 1920s in the United States were referred to as “Depression children,” so too it may be said that Kanzô grew up a “Restoration child.”

His family members were samurai; members of this class ranked above all others in society. The events that followed the Restoration ended samurai dominance and ruined the Uchimuras along with other similar families. The samurai class comprised only about 5 percent of the population and had been formed on the basis of military prowess. Succeeding generations had gradually been entrusted with the functions of civil administration and secular scholarship in addition to defence. More than 200 semi-autonomous government units, or han, plus the Imperial institution at the summit, made up the nation, and each samurai had a role to play in relation to his daimyo, the ruler of his han. For the most part, each samurai exercised this role conscious of his position, his ability, and his responsibility.

During the eight years after the Restoration, samurai gradually lost their function as new institutions replaced those of the old society. With their purpose went their government support. The most gifted samurai moved on to positions in the new society, where their superior training and experience equipped them for whatever opened up. Others could not adjust; instead, they clung to the tattered shreds of the old order, apparently in the faith that some reward would attend their loyalty to an obsolete way of life. Kanzô’s father belonged to this second group.

The members of Kanzô’s family formed his world; his parents, siblings, and more distant relatives taught him how to act and react as a person toward other people. Kanzô learned these skills just as the changes occasioned by the threat of foreign intervention began to wreak havoc on the little world of his family.

Perhaps the most important characteristic of Kanzô’s world was that the men did not seem to act as men; they did not provide the support that gives relaxed confidence to wives and children. Kanzô’s paternal grandfather lived with the family until he died, when Kanzô was four. He remembers his grandfather as the caricature of the samurai, ineffective as a military man in a world that no longer needed him. “He was never so happy as when he appeared in his ponderous armour, decked with [sic] a bamboo-bow and pheasant-feathered arrows and a 50-pound firelock.” Kanzô’s maternal grandfather had died, apparently as a young man, twenty years before Kanzô’s birth. After becoming an adult, Uchimura recorded that his mother’s father was “essentially an honest man” because, when constrained to accept a loan from an overlord, he paid the high interest out of his own pocket. In such circumstances, many samurai forced numbers of those under them to accept such money in smaller loans at even higher rates of interest. Uchimura points with pride to both his grandfather’s honesty and his total abstinence from liquor. But increasing poverty marked Kanzô’s boyhood, and to a boy the same traits might well have connoted more a lack of manliness than a concern with doing the right thing.

Neither the boy Kanzô nor the man Uchimura could characterize his father Yoshiyuki so easily. In his autobiographical How I Became a Christian, Uchimura fondly recalls Yoshiyuki’s ability as a scholar and tutor, but other sources indicate how, as Kanzô grew up, he considered his father ineffectual. Although when Kanzô was an adolescent Yoshiyuki seemed weak, as a young man he had showed considerable promise. The rank of the Uchimura family within the samurai class was umamawari; this rank carried a modest hereditary stipend that enabled the family to live in comfortable but not luxurious circumstances. What we know of the abilities of Yoshiyuki’s father would indicate that this sum, though fixed by custom, accorded well with his actual contribution to society. The early professional record of Yoshiyuki himself reflected much more capability. Among other things, he knew military affairs and early recommended the modernization of his han’s army. The system of hereditary rank possessed enough flexibility so that an able man could rise in the administrative structure above his traditional family status. At the time of Kanzô’s birth, Yoshiyuki was about thirty; he appears to have been then in the service of his daimyo as a kind of personal secretary in the capital, Edo, which would later become Tokyo. The various han, in many ways autonomous states within the world of Japan, maintained establishments in Edo. They acted like embassies in negotiations with the central government, and the men attached to Edo offices represented the more able elements in their han. Yoshiyuki’s daimyo, Ôkôchi Teruna of Takasaki han, which lay at the foot of the mountains to the west of Edo, thought highly of the elder Uchimura.

When Kanzô was five, Yoshiyuki was given four new assignments; the title of each implied considerable responsibility. The preferment did not last long. Within seven months, he was relieved of his position and sent back to a small city within the han itself. There he worked at tasks of much less import. It is not known what happened, but the move appears to have resulted from Yoshiyuki’s recommendation that the han’s military forces be Westernized. Such a move would have evoked ready opposition from other samurai whose rank gave them a vested interest in the old system. In any case, the family moved from the bustle of the national capital to a quiet provincial city. There they rusticated until a few months after the Restoration.

Then fortune smiled once more. In the initial confusion caused by the Restoration, the new central government shared political responsibility with the former daimyo. As part of the accommodation, the central government chose top officials, and the former daimyo chose the administrative assistants of secondary rank. Ôkôchi Teruna called Yoshiyuki out of his semiretirement and made him one of these assistants in an area that Takasaki had been assigned to administer but had not ruled traditionally. It was the highest position that Ôkôchi could bestow. For the next few years, Yoshiyuki survived several more changes. Each time he moved into positions that had formerly been filled by men of higher rank. He changed his given name perhaps, as was the custom, to accord with his good fortune. The family moved to be with him. This transfer of the Uchimura family from Takasaki west of Tokyo to Ishimaki far to the north of Tokyo remained a happy memory for Uchimura. The move took twelve days. For the five members of the family, there were palanquins, each attended by three carriers, as well as servants and younger assistants of his father, so that it was “quite a party.” Kanzô remembers that on the way they picked and ate chestnuts growing along the road by leaning out of their palanquins. What a trip for an elementary school boy!

For a while, Kanzô’s father had complete responsibility for a province. It was the high point of his career. Many years later Uchimura ruminated that, since his father had been a provincial governor at this time, “if all had gone well,” he would have become at least a baron in the new Western-style peerage established a few years later by the Meiji government. This was not to happen. Before Yoshiyuki could really settle down in this job, Ôkôchi Teruna recalled him. Yoshiyuki returned out of personal loyalty, though he probably could have stayed where he was. The name of his position back in Takasaki remained the same, but his new duties did not provide him with the same opportunity to display his abilities. After a short time, the central government relieved Ôkôchi of his temporary power, with the result that there was almost nothing for Yoshiyuki to do. He was shifted again to a much lower position. In 1872, he was retired; he was just over forty, and his official career had ended. Kanzô was eleven. Yoshiyuki tried to farm for a while and then bought a house in Tokyo, as Edo had been renamed, with the remainder of his severance money. For seven years as Kanzô was in his twenties, Yoshiyuki served in the Tokyo home of Ôkôchi, but aside from that he did practically nothing to support the family. He remained at home, “reading books, composing poems, playing go,” and until he became a Christian under the influence of Kanzô “drinking sake.”

To the adolescent Kanzô, his father’s career must have seemed a failure – but not one due entirely to his own inability. If it is true that Yoshiyuki had suffered because of his proposal to modernize the han military forces, his son would have realized that his father had been punished because he had been ahead of his times. The speedy adoption of Western military techniques was one of the cornerstones of the new official Restoration policy. Moreover, Yoshiyuki had moved from his position of greatest responsibility to one of much less responsibility at the behest of his feudal overlord, even though his compliance with Ôkôchi’s wishes had hurt his own career. No act could have done him more credit under the code that he honoured. Yet neither native ability nor ethical rectitude enabled him to support his family. His devotion to his lord, so esteemed under the old dispensation, later became a cruel farce, for in the 1880s Ôkôchi had no work for him to do and very little with which to reward his touching loyalty. Uchimura refers with pride to Yoshiyuki’s ability to “repeat from memory almost every passage in the writings and sayings” of Confucius, but this ability could not have seemed to young Kanzô a fit substitute for an income.

While Kanzô was still in his teens, his father started to depend on him. Yoshiyuki made Kanzô the head of the household when the boy was sixteen. Although early retirement characterized Japanese society, and in some families even retirement at this age might have been considered normal, Yoshiyuki’s own father had not turned over authority to Yoshiyuki before he died. When Kanzô started to receive a stipend as a governmentsupported student within a year after he took over, much of this income went to his family. A few years later Kanzô converted his father to Christianity. The mature Uchimura recalls that Yoshiyuki put up quite a struggle, but the evidence that he presents for his opinion indicates that as soon as he could be persuaded to read the Bible Yoshiyuki gave in to his son’s entreaties. A few months after he had converted his father, Kanzô graduated from college, and soon thereafter as a young official he adopted a patronizing air toward his father. “Visit him at your leisure, I pray you,” Kanzô wrote to a classmate who was also Christian. “Speak to him what I now write to you. Pray for him at your opportunity.” Perhaps this attitude reflected unconscious awareness that Yoshiyuki had not provided the support and discipline that Kanzô had desired.

Kanzô’s maternal grandmother and his mother were the women in his young life. His grandmother, widowed by her overgenerous spouse a score of years before Kanzô’s birth, was remembered by Uchimura as a workhorse: “She was born to work – vivare est laborare for her and for forty years she did work as any frail human could work.” Uchimura saw in his mother a replica of her own mother. She “inherited from her mother this mania for work. She forgets all the pains and sorrows of life in her work. She ... ‘can’t afford’ to be gloomy because life is hard. Her little home is her Kingdom, and she rules it ... as no queen has ever done.” She must have appeared to be very strong and efficient. But underneath she perhaps felt insecure in part because she had been born blind in one eye and sought someone upon whom she could depend. She had a superstitious regard for some of the tenets of Buddhism, and as Kanzô grew to manhood she seems to have turned to him to satisfy her longing for a man who would provide some protection against the world. She spent her final days in a mental institution, and Uchimura’s later recollections of her problems aggravated his occasional concern about his own sanity. Neither one of these women could have expressed to the young Kanzô much affection for him or for the other men in the family; they also probably did not instill in him much of a sense of respect or trust for either his father or his grandfathers. As the men in the family defaulted on their responsibilities, the women and the eldest son felt increased responsibility. The mother and grandmother had no time for womanly grace or affection, and Kanzô felt deprived of it.

Perhaps in reaction, from an early age he adopted the elements of religion available to him to help control his environment. Kanzô did not get his piety from his father, who, before he became a Christian, “was decidedly blasphemous toward heathen gods of all sorts.” He once challenged the gods as he threw a small coin into a collection box, telling them that “they would have another such coin if they would in any way help him to win a law-case in which he was then engaged.” This was, Uchimura adds, “a feat wholly beyond my power at any period of my religious experience.”

In direct contrast to his father, Kanzô regarded religions and their demands seriously. He liked to play Buddhist priest until his father dissuaded him and then turned his mind to Shinto observances. He imitated the Shinto priests in his games. While he played at praying in the presence of other children, he often appeared to forget that it was only a game.How I Became a Christian also engagingly describes the pain caused by the conflicting dietary prescriptions of various gods and the circuitous path that the young boy took to bypass temples and thereby avoid the affront that improper expressions of respect to the deities they honoured might provoke. He really believed that the gods could harm him and that he could ensure their friendship by his boyish precautions. Kanzô projected his own fears onto those around him and treated associates as if he knew better than they themselves did what was good for them.

Little is known of his siblings other than that he found them difficult. He had three brothers and one sister. The three brothers all became teachers, two at mission-supported schools in Japan and the third in the United States. The sister married a provincial banker who had been attracted to the family by Uchimura’s writings. His position as eldest and later head of the family gave Kanzô the right in Japanese society to lord it over his siblings, but his particular need to order their lives seems to have provoked more antagonism than was customary even under the circumstances. A quarter of a century after Kanzô’s death we are told that one of the brothers still refused to meet anyone who came “to talk about Kanzô.” Kanzô felt closer to his next younger brother, Tatsusaburô, than to the others. Tatsusaburô lived with Kanzô to save money for a short time after Kanzô graduated from college; later he also became a writer, and the two brothers cooperated on the staff of a magazine. This cooperation did not continue; by the time of their parents’ deaths, early in the twentieth century, the brothers had become completely estranged. Tatsusaburô attended the burial of neither parent, and Kanzô had to assume complete responsibility. He thought that Tatsusaburô slandered him behind his back on both occasions.

It seems to be safe to assume that Kanzô’s early attempt to order the lives of his siblings and his later assumption of responsibility for his parents cost Kanzô the respect of the other children and irritated them. His cautious acts on behalf of those nearest to him resulted from his own fears and induced dissent rather than harmony. It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the Uchimura home as Kanzô experienced it lacked the grace and warmth that one likes to think provide the best matrix for the young.

Yet in a number of respects, his home gave Kanzô just what he needed. In his later years, Uchimura became an affectionate husband and father, and he must have learned many of the techniques that such expressions of affection require at home as a child. He also gained either from his parents’ genes or from life with them both the ambition that later drove him to success and the aptitude for language by which he effected that success. His father, conscious of his own lack of success, urged Kanzô to succeed in government where he himself had failed. His mother’s need for support gave this ambition a sense of practical urgency. And the father, precisely because he had failed, remained around the house and could act as a tutor. He imparted to his son his love for learning along with his considerable knowledge of Japanese cultural tradition. His own impotence before the forces brought in by the West also provided persuasive evidence for his son that knowledge of the West held the key to both family and national security. This “fretful timid child” hoped that he could discharge his responsibilities and make his place in the world through his use of the foreigner’s skills and particularly their language. He liked to study, and he would discover that he had a way with languages. In his attempt to master the English language, Kanzô received a particular education. At the same time, it equipped him for a position of national leadership and cut him off from much of what his fellow Japanese held dear. Kanzô could not realize it, but his personal decision fitted in with broad national policies that the officials of the new government had drafted.

Their recognition of Japan’s inferiority before the West had prompted them to seek new knowledge from the West, and to accomplish their aim they needed men fluent in Western languages. They considered these languages to be tools that differed only in degree from the many mechanical devices that they were importing. In this they erred, for the Japanese and Western tongues differed so greatly that in the process of real mastery the student became a different person. Young Japanese who gained fluency in English discovered, as Westerners who gained fluency in Japanese were later to discover, that in the process of their accomplishment they themselves had changed. Kanzô set out to acquire a new weapon, and he discovered too late that this weapon, once mastered, had in fact mastered him.

He received his first training in English before his family moved from Takasaki to Tokyo. As early as 1869, the daimyo, Ôkôchi Teruna, enjoyed European wine and possessed a Japanese-English dictionary, at the time symbols of considerable sophistication in the face of Western incursion. Shortly thereafter he started an English-language school. Its teachers first acquainted Kanzô with the mysteries of the new language in 1872. The following year he continued his study at a private school in Tokyo, and in 1874, at the age of thirteen, he was admitted to the government-sponsored Tokyo School of Foreign Languages. From that point on, he received the best training that his society could afford.

In the Tokyo School of Foreign Languages and the Tokyo School of English Language that developed out of it, Kanzô first came into contact with men who later assumed roles of national importance. Katô Takaaki, later to become prime minister, had entered one year ahead of Kanzô. Kanzô’s own class included two boys who would achieve world renown and figure prominently in his own life as personal friends. They were Nitobe Inazô, who became a leading scholar, international civil servant, and interpreter of Japan abroad, and Miyabe Kingo, who later achieved fame as a botanist. As young men, they were Kanzô’s closest friends. Like the rest of the students in the school, they moved on as they matured to become national leaders. Kanzô considered them his peers and shared their aspirations.

In this school, Kanzô also seems to have met individual foreigners for the first time. For most Japanese of his generation, these strangers remained a race apart, but he could view a number of them at close range. He met several different types. One man, an ineffective tippler of the sort who infested Far Eastern port cities, had been employed to teach arithmetic. When an eager student inquired about fractions, he replied with a toss of the hand, “Fractions? I don’t understand them at all.” Another teacher named M.M. Scott had come from Kentucky to teach English. He succeeded so well in his composition classes that his name was revered for generations. On Sundays, Kanzô sometimes amused himself with walks down to the Tsukiji Concession, where he could observe representatives of another group, the missionaries. There, the mature Uchimura recalls, he heard “pretty women sing, and a tall big man with long beard shout and howl upon an elevated place, flinging his arms and twisting his body in all fantastic manners.”

As early as his thirteenth year, Kanzô had met in these various individuals the prototypes of foreigners as he would interpret them throughout his life. Missionaries, with their lack of knowledge of the customs and language of the land to which they went, became a symbol of insufficient respect for the people among whom they worked. The tippler who did not know his job became a symbol for the lack of discipline and ability among certain Westerners. Other members of both groups Kanzô later met would feel a sting of invective from him far disproportionate to anything they had said or done as individuals. They would find him very rude. But to the extent that Uchimura rebuked the men he did not respect, he looked up to the foreigners he did respect as superior human beings. Scott was probably the first among those in this group. Kanzô’s attitudes toward foreigners form an important theme of this study, and, inasmuch as they have their roots in his personal experience, they date from his student years.

In this school, the students gained the tools that they needed for work with an important group of Westerners. When they left the school, its graduates had enjoyed maximum contact with speakers of English, had studied a number of courses in English, and could express themselves passably in it. Their mastery of such a tool assured them of successful careers. Most, like Kanzô, anticipated a future in the government, and their training made them so valuable that within the government many agencies vied for their services. One of them, the Colonization Office (Kaitakushi), sent a persuasive member of its staff to Tokyo to recruit students for the new agricultural college that it had established in Hokkaido. This man had studied in the United States and now served as the interpreter for the American who had come to help establish the college. He assured his prospects that the mechanisms of civilization would protect them against the rigors of the northern winter and promised them large stipends. The students all wanted to go, but only three obtained the permission of their parents. They were Nitobe, Miyabe, and Kanzô.

Kanzô in particular appreciated the prospect of good pay. Since Yoshiyuki had made his son head of the family, the responsibility seems to have weighed heavily on him. The previous year a bout with pleurisy had kept him home from school much of the time, and concern over his responsibilities may have increased his susceptibility to it. To learn agricultural techniques in Sapporo might frustrate the political ambitions that Kanzô shared with his father, but in exchange it would provide much needed financial relief.

In 1877, Kanzô set sail from Tokyo for Sapporo far to the north with a number of others. There they found themselves influenced in a far different manner from what they had anticipated. Three factors combined to bring about great changes in their lives. They were the interaction of the two strong personalities who had together developed the college, the physical and ethical institutions that these two had decided should inform its instruction, and the new faith that one of them condoned and the other actively fostered. These men were Kuroda Kiyotaka and William S. Clark. An understanding of the roles that these two men played in the college makes it easier to comprehend what happened to Kanzô there.

Kuroda came from the han of Satsuma, where he had early distinguished himself as a military leader. Satsuma in company with a few other han had led the plots and campaigns to overthrow the previous Tokugawa government. Kuroda had commanded the final operation of the war in Hakodate on the southern coast of Hokkaido. There the ragged partisans of the Tokugawa had holed themselves up within modern coastal defences that their government had designed to ward off invasion from Western fleets. Kuroda had breached these defences; then, with a magnanimity unusual for the time, he had spared the life of the defeated general. Perhaps this experience in Hokkaido had whetted his interest in its problems. In any case, just twelve months after the war ended, he took charge of the area that consisted almost entirely of virgin forest. He was thirty years old. After a trip abroad, he drafted a program for the systematic development of Hokkaido.

In the formation of his plan, Kuroda spent much time considering how to train young Japanese technically qualified to work in Hokkaido. He himself started a school for boys in 1872, but it did not produce the kind of men he wanted. The first group of students he expelled in a fit of anger when they did not study. Other students were selected and given more intensive ethical training in the hope that it would make them work harder, but they also disappointed him. He decided that life in Tokyo could not condition men for work in Hokkaido and determined to reestablish the school in its new capital, Sapporo. Once settled there, the students applied themselves to more productive study and soon outstripped the capabilities of their faculty. Kuroda requested the Foreign Ministry to find him “three Americans” to supplement the Japanese faculty members so that he could provide the higher education for which the students were now prepared.

Yoshida Kiyonari, the Japanese consul in the United States, asked the president of the Massachusetts Agricultural College at Amherst to go himself and select some others to accompany him. Both Amherst College and the Agricultural College had already trained a number of Japanese students. Japanese government missions had visited the institutions and met their presidents, so the Japanese knew that the Agricultural College was the first of its kind and a nationally recognized leader. Yoshida had come to the right place, and he felt happy when its president, William S. Clark, acceded to his request.

It is difficult to evaluate Clark’s contribution in Japan on the basis of his later experience in the United States. Japan spoiled Clark. When he returned to the Agricultural College after less than a year, its routine of administration bored him. He tried to establish a “floating university” that would take students on an extended cruise for their college years, teach them in the process, and return them to a New York pier with their degrees. In the attempt to finance this scheme, Clark squandered most of his own resources and those of his neighbours. He died less than a decade later unlamented by most of his fellow townspeople and convinced that he had done his greatest work in Japan. Although the university recognizes him as the individual who contributed more than anybody else in its formative years, shortly after the end of the Second World War its president could locate, only with difficulty, Clark’s grave for visiting Japanese officials who had come from Boston to express their respects before it.

Few Americans ever hear of Clark; like Will Adams, whose adventures have been publicized in James Clavell’s Shogun, Clark made his greatest contribution in Japan rather than in his native land. But what these few Americans hear of Clark – that he told “boys” to be “ambitious,” for instance – is likely to strike them as more insipid than inspiring. The words echo a bumptious enthusiasm that no longer commands respect in Clark’s homeland.

The inability to share Clark’s enthusiasm should not blind us from the recognition that Yoshida could not have found a better man at the time. Study in both the United States and Germany had given Clark the best professional training that his generation could afford, and the Agricultural College that so reflected his leadership represented just what the Japanese wanted. As an individual, he was also the kind of man Kuroda sought. His height and stance gave him an air of authority, and his command of local volunteers in the Civil War had provided him with the military experience so valued in Japan. His integrity and interest in ethical instruction made him even more valuable.

Not visible either to Japanese or to most of his fellow Americans were other characteristics that proved to be important in Japan. As a student at Amherst College in 1849, Clark had experienced a deep religious conversion during a period of revival, and though he did not appear unusually pious to his colleagues he shared the interest of many of his New England contemporaries in missionary work in Japan. Mrs. Clark was the daughter of an early missionary to Hawaii and seems herself to have been half Polynesian. It is not surprising that a man of personal piety and acquaintance with the fruits of missionary outreach should want to make of the appointment to teach agriculture to young Japanese an opportunity to evangelize. Clark did not tell Yoshida that he would proselytize his students; perhaps he himself did not even think of it.

The terms on which Clark acceded to the request reflect at once his estimate of his ability and the Japanese government’s desire to get him. He agreed to bring two of his assistants with him on the understanding that he would spend one year away from Amherst and that they would stay on. He was to be the “president” of the new college. Although in the official Japanese documents he is referred to as the “head of instruction” (kyôtô) under a Japanese principal, the Colonization Office responded to his every whim as if he was in charge. He was to receive $7,200 for his year, and his assistants would receive something less than half that. These salaries were very high. Clark’s share amounted to almost 50 percent more than the salary of the governor of Massachusetts, and his assistants each received about as much as the president of Amherst College. Midway through the negotiations, the Japanese officials became concerned about not getting their money’s worth. They asked Clark through a personal friend whether he thought he could achieve enough in only one year. He replied with characteristic assurance that he could impart two years’ worth of the necessary information within one year’s time.

The three Americans arrived in Tokyo in the summer of 1877. After they selected students there, Kuroda, the new faculty members, and the students – including girls, for whom a separate school had been provided – travelled together by ship to Hokkaido. On board, Kuroda took Clark’s measure. He liked what he saw, and events on the trip made him decide to request that Clark teach ethics as well as agriculture. An oft-repeated anecdote describes the particular way that events led him to this decision. One day as the two were conversing, they overheard some of the male students complain that the girls had been given preferred berthing space. Kuroda took this as evidence that the boys were no better than the group he had earlier dismissed in Tokyo. His aides dissuaded him only with difficulty from his decision to send the offenders home at once, but he continued to worry about how to provide them with ethical instruction. His own talents lay more in military strategy and government administration than in education, and his experience with inculcating ethics could not inspire confidence in his own judgment. He asked Clark to take on the extra task. Clark accepted on the condition that he be allowed to use the Bible as the basis of instruction. Kuroda, of course, refused the condition. His government’s policy was to emphasize native ethics as the basis of training, and its leaders saw the Bible as antithetical to native tradition. Clark refused Kuroda’s repeated requests until Kuroda gave in only hours before the opening ceremony in Sapporo.

Dramatic variations of this story enliven Japanese accounts of the Sapporo experience. The two military men are seen in direct confrontation; the subsequent Japanese defeat is unlamented, apparently because of Clark’s great contributions to Japanese development. Although it may not seem to be important and most certainly is untrue in many details, while as a general outline of attitudes it is correct, the incident tells us much about the crisis in confidence that beset many men like Kuroda. His own homilies to the students in Tokyo had proved ineffective. On the other hand, he admired Clark and trusted his judgment. In granting Clark permission to teach Christianity, he unleashed forces he could neither control nor understand. He himself, according to one account, had murdered his wife, and assignment to the Colonization Office became kind of an exile to keep an embarrassment to the new oligarchs out of sight and mind. True or not, Kuroda had matured under the old order, so he could not imagine what ambivalence might be introduced into the students’ lives by exposure in such surroundings to a whole new ethical world. Clark also could not comprehend the psychological effects of his action. The students themselves would not fully comprehend them for a number of years.

Although Clark’s strength of character remains the one element in the Sapporo experience that is best remembered, in the college there were other equally persuasive forces that worked to change familiar thought patterns. Kuroda and Clark together worked out a program of institutions specifically designed to teach students what Western civil servants had to know and to disabuse them of the samurai ethics that no longer served any useful purpose. Even without Clark’s injection of Christianity, the students faced an experience very akin to what would later be called brainwashing.

A description of Kanzô’s life in Sapporo will show how the surroundings there and these new institutions affected the young Uchimura. He arrived with his two friends Nitobe and Miyabe, among others, in 1877, one year after Kuroda and Clark had opened the college. They debarked at Otaru, the port for Sapporo, and then rode horseback for a day to Sapporo itself. There they eased their saddle-weary limbs to the ground in a rude community that had been laid out in the grid pattern characteristic of American frontier towns.

A wood-block print shows the city as it existed a few years later. It included a number of handsome, two-storey buildings; the main one had a clock tower. An earthen wall surrounded the wide grounds on which the buildings sat. In the print, clouds frame this scene; a conventional part of woodblock technique, the clouds served incidentally to screen the observer from the void that lay roundabout. The only other building of any eminence in the city housed the government headquarters, and from its tower one could get a good view of the surrounding mountains. A racetrack complemented the low homes of the townspeople. There was little else. That the population was about 3,000 was worthy of note only to those who knew that it had grown from two families in less than ten years. Not far from the school, the woods began. When Kanzô and the others arrived, the surroundings were even more rustic since many of the buildings and the clock tower in particular went up after they arrived. Kanzô once shot snipe from a dormitory window. On another occasion, he ran to pick up the quarry that Kuroda had downed while hunting, and one spring night a starving bear attacked a settler’s home within walking distance and made off with some young children. The few people in the community had only one another for human companionship.

In this small frontier town, the school formed an even smaller community. There the students lived in a manner little related, either physically or intellectually, to the world that they glimpsed over the school wall. Their wooden tower isolated them more than most ivory towers set other scholars apart. It transported them to what seemed a glamorous and faraway world.

Kanzô and the others had received their first issue of school uniforms from the government before they left Tokyo. The style of cloth and cut was entirely Western. The standard issue included three pairs of shoes, each of a different height. It also included a complete outfit of underclothing and night suits. A photograph shows some of the students in their summer uniforms, which look rumpled even though they were new. But no matter how the suits looked or felt, they served as a badge of proud distinction. A few days before his graduation, one of the boys wore Japanese clothes on his way to the bath. It was so infrequent a practice that he recorded the fact in his diary.

The students thus attired in Western dress lived in rooms like those of American college students. Walls that were fifteen feet on a side enclosed ample space for two students, each of whom had a Western-style bed, desk, chair, and lamp; they shared the care and the warmth of a small stove. Although they dressed, worked, and slept as Westerners, the students did not have to eat entirely as Westerners. They received Japanese food for lunch. But the rest of the time they also learned to eat food like that of their Western contemporaries on the frontier. Breakfast consisted of meat served with thick slices of toast that the hungry young men heaped with butter and sugar. The evening meal included soup, a meat or fish stew, and more thick slices of bread. Most frequently, the deer that roamed the nearby woods provided the meat; an order for 100 quarters of venison indicates both how much could be used before it spoiled and how much was available.

These details reflect how completely material surroundings like those of the American frontier dominated student life. Although perhaps the source of some inconvenience at first, they were quickly accepted. In this case, unlike what happened in America, Western material culture did not exist alone; a determined attempt to incorporate Western values accompanied it.

First, the students learned to accept middle-class attitudes toward money. Both Kuroda and Clark knew how much trouble money gave samurai families. Many of them had suffered in the same way as the Uchimuras. Samurai had always received stipends before the Restoration, and, after the Restoration, pride of former position and inability to do any useful work prevented them from learning how to accumulate or use money. In Sapporo, the boys were paid and were helped to husband carefully what they received. Each got sixteen yen a month in addition to board and keep. This amount came to twice what the government allotted the college each month for their food, and all that they had to buy out of it was soap, postage, and stationery. Second, they received an hourly wage for their work in the school experimental fields and could retain any profit from the plots of land that each tilled. And third, they could earn cash for academic excellence; the upper limit on this was twenty-two yen per year.

Having earned the money did not entitle the students to dispose of it as they pleased. It went straight into accounts in their names. Each received an allowance of twenty sen – one-fifth of a yen – each Saturday. This gave them pocket money for walks outside the college compound. The rest they could claim at any time if they could convince the authorities that they needed it, and any remainder would go to them upon graduation.

Kanzô learned to handle money very well. His income averaged about twenty-two yen per month from these various sources. With this sum, he assisted his parents considerably even though he bought expensive books. The experience in Sapporo helped to confirm in him the bourgeois values that marked his later life. The religious thinker in him never conflicted with both a sound business sense and a self-image as a member of the middle class.

In addition to these attitudes toward money, the students learned how to enjoy the outdoors and how to work with their hands. Clark occasionally appeared in the dormitories to pry them loose from their books. He also instructed them in gymnastics, military drill, and personal hygiene. Practical work in the fields further ingrained in them the satisfactions of outdoor manual labour. Graduates of Sapporo would not be, in the famous words of Fukuzawa Yukichi, mere “rice-eating dictionaries.” In later life, Kanzô loved hiking, biking, and swimming. His delight in these exercises seems to date from his years in Sapporo. Although the attitudes toward money and exercise that he learned in Sapporo influenced Kanzô greatly, neither influence shaped his later life as much as the religious conviction that he gained there. When the students went into their classroom for the first time, each found an English-language Bible on the desk. This became their text for instruction in ethics. These Bibles were part of a group of thirty that Clark had received in Yokohama before Kuroda had even asked him to teach ethics. Clark’s dedication matched his foresight. Clark not only encouraged the students to accept Christianity but himself exemplified what seemed to him to be the best in Christian virtues. He had brought along, for instance, some tobacco and liquor, but after he accepted the task of ethical instruction he publicly destroyed them. In him, the little Western world of the campus gained both Christianity and a self-denying advocate of it, and the other foreign teachers continued to exercise similar influence after he went home.

In this atmosphere, Kanzô grew into a very different person: on the one hand confident, capable, and overbearing, on the other dependent and alone. The situation worked to emphasize characteristics already formed and worked on what was, after all, a young mind. Kanzô had lived only sixteen years before he went to Sapporo, and he shared all the normal needs of a homesick young man. Prominent among the problems that assailed him were the fear of responsibility and the need for affection. Both were aggravated by the power of words in a situation in which he had to work in a foreign language and live in a small and controlled, almost monastic, society.

Shortly after Kanzô arrived, he was asked to sign two pledges. Both were in a tradition shared by nineteenth-century American Protestantism and the Japanese administrative system in which individuals often pledged themselves to do, or more likely not to do, some act deemed to have ethical significance. In theory, their signatures rendered individuals better equipped to resist temptation even though the frequency with which pledges were required seems to attest to their inability to improve permanently those who signed them.

Kanzô affixed his signature to the first of the two almost immediately. Drafted by the young teachers after Clark had left, it bound its signatories to refrain from using tobacco and liquor. No compunctions seem to have slowed Kanzô’s hand. Neither habit ever attracted the young man. Since he had seen how his father’s drinking of sake had eaten into the family’s slim resources at home, he probably had strong ideas similar to those of the American teachers, so this first pledge required nothing of him but to reaffirm previous conviction.

The second pledge was not so innocuous. Clark himself had penned it shortly before his departure. It was called the “Covenant of Believers in Jesus.” Clark seems to have based it upon the covenant of an independent church in Brooklyn, New York, with which he had been affiliated. It said, in part, “The undersigned ... desiring to confess Christ according to his command, do solemnly covenant with God and with each other from this time forth to be his faithful disciples, and to live in strict compliance with the letter and the spirit of his teachings; and whenever a suitable opportunity offers we promise to present ourselves for examination, baptism and admission to some evangelical church.” In short, signing pledged Kanzô to turn his back almost completely on what he had held dear up to that time. He had many reasons not to sign.

In the first place, to sign seemed unpatriotic. Until four years earlier, all Christianity had been outlawed for more than 200 years. In the sixteenth century, Japan’s rulers had become convinced that aggressive foreign arms would follow the Catholic missionaries who were then enjoying great success. Fearful authorities outlawed Christianity in self-defence, for to them Christians seemed as dangerous as Communists would seem in the twentieth-century Mississippi Valley, and for many of the same reasons. Kanzô had another reason to hesitate. If he became a Christian, it would seem like the final blow to his family’s samurai status. Until the early seventeenth century, they had been farmers and had achieved their coveted rank because one of them had brought to bear superior marksmanship in the suppression of the seventeenth-century revolt led by Christians at Shimabara in Kyushu.

In addition to these reasons of family and nation, Kanzô had personal cause to hesitate. His convictions stemming from popular religions would not let him sign. His life revolved around the demands of the gods and spirits intimately associated with Japan, and to the extent that he believed in their efficacy he could anticipate their malice if he abandoned them.

Although to sign would invite the displeasure of the gods, the covenant also promised that future benefits would follow upon signature. Its last paragraph outlined the nature of the community of believers into which the faithful entered. It said, “For mutual assistance and encouragement we hereby constitute ourselves an association under the name ‘Believers in Jesus,’ and we promise faithfully to attend one or more meetings each week while living together, for the reading of the bible or other religious books or papers, for conference and for social prayer; and we sincerely desire the manifest presence in our hearts of the Holy Spirit to quicken our love, to strengthen our faith, and to guide us into a saving knowledge of the truth.” Here was compensation of a sort for what one lost in renunciation of the past. Kanzô felt the need of a close-knit community in Sapporo. He probably already felt how his special training set him apart from the commonality of his fellow students. If he could find among the Christians a brotherhood to make up for the sense of identity he had earlier felt with the samurai, all the better. More than this, his ambition would have made him realize at once that Christianity might be the faith of the future both for him and for all humanity. To join at once would align a young man early with the tides of history.

It is impossible to know the complex of motivations that played upon Kanzô at the time, but it is clear that the decision followed quite a struggle and that until his capitulation he led the group who refused to give in. Reasons very acceptable by adolescent standards are given in his reminiscences for his final submission: he says that a “religion-rush, not cane-rush,” by the sophomores finally made him capitulate. When students at the time entered American institutions of higher education in America, they were often beat with canes by more senior students as a form of initiation. All the members of the earlier class had fallen prey to Clark’s spell and signed. They had been baptized the night that Kanzô and his group had arrived. Now the upperclassmen aimed to convert others in a kind of religious Freshman Week. A perceptive student of Uchimura’s life, Arima Tatsuo, has found Uchimura’s reason “not very convincing.” Other evidence supports his skepticism and forms the basis for the following account.

First, the upperclassmen, as arbiters of student mores in this little world, apparently presented the new students with little choice. Since the upperclassmen had just been baptized, they were themselves too insecure to put up with diversity, and any student who did not become a Christian would, by his or her intransigence, threaten the faith of those who had already signed. The objects of such evangelical zeal could easily confuse it with hazing. Kanzô withstood the onslaught until the second of his two close friends gave in. Nitobe had been deeply influenced by Christianity before he left Tokyo, and he signed shortly after he arrived in September. Miyabe gave in three months later after long soul-searching. Their conversion threatened to leave Kanzô alone. To fail to sign would not cost him friends in general as much as the friendships of these other leaders. It was they, after all, who had persuaded the officials in Tokyo to let him go to Sapporo in spite of his history of recent pleurisy. He could not stand alone without their support. His ambition to be with them and his need for affection from them overcame his patriotic scruples. He signed the day after Miyabe signed. Within a few days, the remaining members of his class who did give in, a total of seven, had affixed their names.

Six months later, in June 1878, an American missionary, M.C. Harris, baptized Kanzô and the other six. Harris, who represented the MethodistEpiscopal denomination in Hakodate, had made the daunting trip to Sapporo to baptize the boys. At twenty-eight, he was a warm and understanding man, generous in his appreciation of others, and therefore much like an older brother. Uchimura never lost his affection for Harris, but he appreciated Mrs. Harris even more. She understood him and helped him when he needed it most. Sometimes her help took practical form. She corrected his writing style and found a publisher for his first English-language article. At other times, she helped him to see how pompous he appeared when he took himself too seriously; she even made him thank her for her chiding. In his eulogy written after her death in 1909, Uchimura found that her only fault had been that “she loved Japan too much,” and her great contribution to him had been as “my friend.” The Harrises became the first among the foreigners Kanzô met that live on in tradition as great spiritual leaders and benefactors of him and through him of the Japanese people.

Almost immediately the seven fledgling Christians set about to create a new brotherhood of believers. They hoped to give practical form to their pledge to quicken love, strengthen faith, and guide each other into “a saving knowledge of the truth.” After the baptism ceremony, Uchimura later recalled, each of the new Christians chose a Christian name from a Webster’s dictionary. Nitobe chose Paul because, as a student of literature, he admired Paul’s writings, Miyabe chose Francis, and Kanzô chose Jonathan, because “I was a strong advocate of the virtue of friendship, and Jonathan’s love for David pleased me well.” At a time when Kanzô needed friends, he found them – or rather continued with them – in his new faith.

The boys who had been baptized together immediately formed themselves into a “church” very similar in their eyes to the apostolic church. Each in turn assumed the responsibilities of a minister. The one appointed on a particular Sunday cleaned up his room, arranged blankets on the floor, brought in the flour barrel that served as a pulpit, and draped it with a blanket. The other members sat before the pulpit, and the minister led them from the eminence of a chair. The service consisted of prayer, Bible reading, a short sermon, and witnesses by members of the group to their faith. Shortly after the inception of the church, Nitobe suggested the addition of refreshments to encourage attendance. He already appreciated the close relation between the stomach and the spirit of even the religious person.

It is clear that this church filled a number of gaps in the lives of the converts. The first gap, of course, was simply time. With their conversion, they took upon themselves the strictures of New England Puritanism, including punctilious observance of the Sabbath. New converts could not do any of the things that they normally would have done on this day. A long church service partially filled the void and utilized excess energies. Bible study with the upperclassmen Sunday evening helped to provide further activity, and a prayer meeting before bed Wednesday night rounded out the program of communal worship.

As the church provided the seven members with a group of intimates, so it set them off as a group apart. They could not even join wholeheartedly with their upper-class Christian brethren. They united with these others for the Wednesday Bible study, but after each joint meeting they retired by themselves for a short conversation before they ended their day.

The “church” in this way served social at least as much as religious ends for its members, who, like other students in their late teens, craved the comforting security of small “in” groups. In the church, they could share their experiences and find strength against the other forces in society.

For Kanzô at least, the six other members of this little circle became, with the passage of time, closer than his blood brothers. As he had chosen his Christian name because he found friendship so important, so letters and the reminiscences of the others about him show how, for the rest of his life, he counted on their support. The most intimate among them remained Miyabe and Nitobe. For a summer, the three of them rose at 5 AM each day and went to a classroom where they read together two or three chapters of the Bible. This way they read through most of the Pentateuch. Kanzô shared a room with Miyabe until graduation, in contravention of the policy that students change their partners regularly. Kingo’s personality complemented Kanzô’s; quiet and scholarly, Kingo possessed a deep and sustaining faith and could abide the angularities of Kanzô because he himself felt secure. They did not argue, and Miyabe recalled as an old man that while they roomed together he was not once the object of Kanzô’s wrath.

Miyabe went on from graduation to study in Tokyo and the United States. After finishing his education, he returned to Sapporo to teach in the new Hokkaido Imperial University that had succeeded the Agricultural College. Uchimura dedicated his greatest work, the study of Paul’s Letter to the Romans, to Miyabe, and in nightmares during his final illness he called out for Miyabe. Miyabe recognized Kanzô’s dependence on those around him and particularly on himself. The presence of this quiet scholar in the city that meant so much to them both over the years provided a haven, both physical and spiritual, for Uchimura. The roughly 200 extant letters from Uchimura to Miyabe form the most intimate of the autobiographical sources.

Nitobe, though also always close to Uchimura, could not support him psychologically as Miyabe did. Fascinated by literature, he read voraciously, and his reading summoned doubts. These doubts made him nervous and edgy as a student, though he matured into positions of national and international trust that he assumed with calm. Although his less secure faith prevented him from providing spiritual support for Uchimura, he did help him in a very practical way early in the twentieth century. As principal of the First Higher School in Tokyo, he introduced Uchimura to some of the students who later became loyal disciples of both men.

The other members of the church occupied a place in Kanzô’s heart only slightly removed from that of Miyabe and Nitobe. Some of them spent two summers in Sapporo together with him camping or running surveys for construction, and the letters from Uchimura that they saved over the years indicate his continued dependence on them.

Although he required constant support from these friends, the young Kanzô could respond only with firm leadership that in effect expressed his need to control those about him. These other six were the group that formed his new little world. They appear to have desired leadership as much as he needed to lead. The later disciples who followed him with even fewer qualms would, to an extent, take the place of the Sapporo friends, so that he always had near him a group of people who looked to him for leadership and accepted his decisions. Although he dictated to the others, Kanzô does not seem to have returned the affection that they showed him. Many of them carefully saved the letters sent to them, but he does not seem to have saved their replies.

The need to control his surroundings spurred Kanzô on to extraordinary achievement in competition with his new siblings. He could not rest unafraid unless he received the best marks in everything. He had a particular ability to get to the “spirit of things” in complex written work; he listened closely, even in fields far removed from his specialty; and he made what he heard and read his own. He carefully prepared all material one week before examinations and then walked for miles as he composed questions and answers. As the instructor wrote the questions on the blackboard, Kanzô started to write furiously. He usually wrote twice as much as anyone else, and he almost always received the best grades. Miyabe’s special interest in botany implies that he should have beaten Kanzô in it. Although Miyabe did his best, when the results were posted, “There it was; I had 93.6, but he had 100.” Some fifty years after the fact, Nitobe recalled to a young assistant that he had felt similar frustration for a similar reason.

By the time of graduation, Kanzô had the highest average in every subject, including deportment, in which for the entire four years he received 100 percent. Given the military regimen that dominated the school, this seems unbelievable. It conjures up visions of a young man almost neurotically preoccupied with doing things the right way, perhaps transferring to the school regulations the same scrupulous concern that he had previously accorded shrines and temples. His perfect mark resulted from conscious control, not natural goodness, for Kanzô had a towering temper that he allowed but slight rein. Miyabe recalls how he handled one tantrum by bursting into the room where Miyabe was studying, picking up an earthenware teapot, and saying, “Miyabe, I’m going to smash this.” After he had dashed it against the floor, he explained that he felt much better and carefully swept up the pieces.

The sense of competition with his new brothers that Uchimura felt continued throughout his life. Later he frequently compared the careers that each of the members of the church had followed after school. The comparison assumed a continuation of the vows that they had made when together and under Kanzô’s control in Sapporo.

In this discussion about the little church as a vehicle for idle energy and the source of a new family for Kanzô, an important element in its appeal remains to be mentioned. In the ethical maxims of Puritanism that accompanied Christianity, the students found much that approximated the best in their old tradition. Perhaps most important were the carefully worked out lists of “dos” and “don’ts” that characterized both Puritanism and Japan’s Confucian society. Among the numerous values that the two shared, the most outstanding was “loyalty.” The difference between the two concepts of loyalty lay in the object of that loyalty and in the nature of the relationship. He who yearned for the affection and authority that the feudal lord had provided his samurai found a ready substitute, at least on the surface, in the Christian God. Once he had tendered this God his loyalty, the strict rules of the Puritan ethic provided welcome support for a mind that continued to require specific rules of behaviour. In the Christianity that Clark bequeathed to the boys, Kanzô found a new set of rules at least as effective as the old ones.

Although the church became a source of psychological support for the boys, this was not the only role that it played in their lives. Wide reading and frequent discussion also taught them much more about their new faith and their God than that acquired by most young men. Kanzô knew the New Testament well in its most literal sense before he left Sapporo, and he and the others had also read widely in classic secondary sources and the popular works on faith that Harris and their other Western friends had passed on to them.

While the church gave the boys a head start on a lifelong interest in the Bible and written sources about their new faith, it gave them little chance to gain an appreciation of Christian tradition as it had developed since biblical times. They missed what regular contact with missionaries and other Westerners provided most young Japanese Christians. Harris did not live in Sapporo but visited only occasionally from Hakodate, more than 100 miles to the south over difficult mountain trails. The American teachers in the college, though they must have known of the student church, do not appear to have treated its members differently from the other students. The young Christians only learned of the custom of grace before meals more than a year after their baptism. While on a journey, Kanzô and Miyabe met a number of Japanese Christians. On one occasion, the others restrained the two visitors from starting to eat before they had returned thanks. They were caught with their chopsticks raised in anticipation. Almost twenty years later Uchimura could remember in his embarrassment every detail of the fish that had lain that day before him awaiting his attack. While in Sapporo, the members of the church had experienced only in the abstract the peculiar way that their universal faith expressed itself in customs developed through centuries of Western tradition. Uchimura later minimized tradition as a factor in Japanese Christianity. This emphasis reflected at least in part his own experience, in which he had found Western Christian traditions of little importance.

Finally, everything that the students learned from their foreign teachers and books came to them through the medium of words that were at best still imperfectly understood. Although Kanzô and the others had started their careers as linguists, even at this time they must have read everything and spoken every word with care. In a sense, all their reading in English and all their conversation with Americans served as advanced language drill. Translators know the abnormal respect for each individual word that their craft demands. They often feel that the search for an equivalent word or expression consumes more time and thought than authors use in their original compositions. The necessity of concentration upon single words in this way increased the impact of the Sapporo experience on those like Kanzô, and the words of the King James Bible helped to mould his own English style and that part of his personality that was Western.

The concentration on words made the Sapporo experience approximate that of a monastic discipline or subjection to thought reform. The students existed in a kind of spiritual hothouse with no other reality besides their little community and with the strain that attends continual dependence on an alien tongue. It was an ideal situation in which to produce deep-seated and lasting psychic change. Nothing seemed more important than their own self-conscious development, yet the further the students pursued this development the farther apart from other Japanese they grew.

The high point of the experience for Kanzô came when he signed the covenant. He could not accept it in the spirit of a sentimental dream for self-improvement. He had to read the words one by one, check their individual meanings, and reassemble them into a whole. He could not escape the recognition that this act made him a different person. He had become a “new man” and had the training along with the outlook appropriate to this status. In general, Kanzô liked himself in this role. For a short time, he lost his sense of foreboding and felt content. His new brothers seemed like a new elect, part of a world elect, who, because of their training, could better fulfill the traditional functions of the samurai within their own society. “Are we not a chosen generation,” Kanzô wrote at the end of his junior year in college, “endowed with privilege to have our eternal hope in God, the Creator of Universe, in vastness, greatness and power?”

Of course, Kanzô wrote in English; it was the language of his new world. “We felt that only with English could we express our innermost emotions and thoughts,” Miyabe wrote more than seventy years later; Kanzô was to find after he refused to bow that in such wholehearted capitulation he had made himself a man divided. In his conversion, he had been born a second time; after he refused to bow, he would feel himself once again a babe. And he would finally resolve only after the First World War the dichotomy of loyalty that his mastery of English had introduced into his life.

But that was all far in the future as he finished his education and started to implement his new skills as a technician charged with the development of Hokkaido. The entry into their individual careers broke up the comforting brotherhood of the little church.
zh: 1903年10月12日正午的汽笛聲響起時，橫須賀海軍造船廠——位於橫濱東邊沿岸——的建築工程聲頓時停止。工人們放下工具，趁著午餐時間休息。其中一位性格深沉、不太善於與同伴相處的年輕人，在他工作的船甲板上找了個僻靜的地方坐下。安頓妥當後，他小心翼翼地打開裝著午餐的報紙，攤開在眼前。那是堅定自由主義立場、極受歡迎的《萬朝報》；這位年輕人想到用報紙來當午間讀物，正是因為報上針砭時弊的言論與他同伴們的看法不合。當他的目光掃過標題時，突然彷彿感到「眼睛被煙火撞擊」了一般。
頭版宣布他最鍾愛的三位專欄作家已經辭職。他們的來信解釋了這個決定。他們說，他們無法同意《萬朝報》贊同政府對俄羅斯的好戰政策。眾人預期戰爭即將爆發。
這位年輕的工作者名叫荒畑寒村，將近六十年後他仍將這個時刻銘記為他人生的轉折點。受到所讀內容的感召，他後來成為日本社會主義運動的先驅之一。許多其他人似乎也在不同程度上受到了《萬朝報》上這些文章的影響。這件事可以說是現代日本思想史上的轉折點之一。
三位專欄作者是幸德傳次郎（秋水）、堺利彥（枯川）和內村鑑三。他們頻繁的投稿為《萬朝報》增添了一種熱烈莊嚴的氣氛。連同報紙後頁上更為聳動的內容，他們幫助這份報紙獲得了日本最大的發行量之一。他們的離去在許多方面都對報紙造成了損害。
一個分明的議題激發了他們的行動。在日益高漲的歇斯底里情緒中——這將導向戰爭——他們全都決定反對戰爭。《萬朝報》的老闆雖然本人同意他們自由主義信條的其他方面，但似乎認為自己不能在這樣的議題上公然反對政府立場。他的專欄作者寧願辭職，也不願放棄己見。他們的行動理應因其所需的勇氣而被銘記。
雖然當時並未立刻顯現，但這一舉動也預示了受基督教影響的日本人之間的分道揚鑣。直到此時，這些論說家既領導著對社會改革感興趣的人們，也領導著關心個人信仰問題的人們。現在幸德秋水和堺利彥轉身離開基督教，去領導社會主義運動。幸德秋水在不到十年後就死在了絞刑架上。他被控密謀暗殺天皇，儘管證據不足。堺利彥後來與荒畑寒村結合，繼續在日益有效的政府反對下，努力喚起人們對社會主義的興趣。

內村曾在《萬朝報》辦公室與幸德秋水和堺利彥並肩工作，參與他們的社會改革方案。辭職後，內村放棄了改造社會的嘗試，轉而專注於個人的改革。他寄望於那些讀他文章、聽他勸誨的人，終有一日會自己成為社會進步的工具。與此同時，他遠離那些主張經濟不平等必然導致革命的人。他在建議一位友人共進午餐時，乾脆地說："不要帶『社會主義者』。"那些急於快速改變社會的人，縱然過去對內村的著述有所認同，也得另尋他處，而不是轉向內村。

雖然他此時的舉動在日本歷史上為他贏得了一席之地，但這裡關心的與其說是它對整個社會的意義，毋寧說是它對內村的意義。在他職業生涯最盛之際，他有意識地、充滿自信地寫下一則便箋，深知這很可能會斷絕他的前程和穩定的收入。他的短信開篇寫道：「我的信念是，與俄國的戰爭將意味著日本的毀滅。」一旦人民決定開戰，他將沒有「勇氣」去反對它，然而作為評論社會事務的人，如果他不表達自己的信念，就將辱沒自己的職業。因此，他決定暫時隱退於社會評論的舞臺。

內村已屆不惑之年。生於責任感重的武士家庭，他曾親眼目睹維新戰爭的某些場景，並終身感受到維新對他的深刻影響。後來，經過訓練以充當日本與威脅性西方列強之間的緩衝，他成為了基督徒，在美國求學，隨後因對一份聲明的尊重態度猶豫不決而成為全國新聞焦點——那份聲明後世的美國人可能會將其比作自己的效忠宣誓。他的膽大妄為使他失去了威望顯赫的政府職位，迫使他作為一名寫手維持一種遠為不穩定的生活。他在《萬朝報》擔任主編的現職，正是因為他對既有體制進行了犀利批評而獲得的。大批讀者欣賞他明確表述的觀點。他將從這個輿論領袖的位置轉身，開啟第二段職業生涯，遠離經濟和政治權力的中心。回顧往昔，內村意識到他童年時曾是一個「煩躁不安、膽小怯懦的孩子」，而這種膽怯似乎與他成長時期家族所遭遇的境況直接相關。三種人格特質在鑑三的青少年時期及成年早期反覆出現。它們如同向量圖中的三股力量一樣構成了三角形的關係。有時一種特質居於主導，有時另一種變得更強，但這三種特質都始終作為他人格構成中的重要因素而存在。這三種特質是：渴望被愛，沉重的責任感，以及支配周圍環境的需要。最後這一特質通過兩種方式表現自身：一時通過某種不分化的恐懼，另一時通過過度的野心。
這種野心似乎是為了使鑑三能夠克服恐懼；他寄望於持續的成功能讓他感到強大和自信。因此他試圖劃定自己的世界範圍，並像開拓者在林間空地上一樣去掌控它——必須保持警戒，以防周圍的草木叢生和其中的生物將他吞沒。
許多人具有這些性格特徵，但鑑三表現得尤為突出，而且持續時間異常之長。沒有人能說清這些特質的特殊組合從何而來；它可能部分源於遺傳，但有理由推測，他成長的社會環境、家庭和學校對他產生了相當大的影響。我將先論述他的家庭背景，再談及他的教育經歷。

鑑三少年時代的重大事件，是伴隨著1868年天皇權力「復辟」而來的日本社會內部勢力重新調整的複雜變化。這個詞指的是經過多代分散的權力之後，權力向國家政府集中。歷史學家們理所當然地爭論這一事件是否真如看起來那樣具有樞紐性的歷史意義。無論如何，對許多經歷過這些變化的人來說，它們似乎構成了他們人生中最重要的事件。那些在舊秩序下屬於特權階級的人為一種令人舒適、根深蒂固的生活方式的終結而悲嘆。這個事件顯得至關重要，而引起這一事件的原因也似乎清晰明瞭：乃是諸西方列強對日本海岸線的衝擊。中央集權的政治運動應運而生，乃是對這一威脅日本主權的衝擊作出的反應，而維新政府最終使日本在西方擴張的浪潮中保持了獨立。愛國的日本人因此無論如何都不能將維新看作是壞事，不管它如何影響了他們個人的生活。他們可能為此感到極度委屈，但是良心上他們只能將隨之而來的敵意指向造成麻煩、導致維新的根源：那些引發一切的外國人。
帝黨宣布意欲將權力歸還天皇，象徵其新的民族主義立場，隨之而來一場短暫的內戰。雙方軍隊前後相繼，在鑑三七歲生日後不久的數月內，曾經過他的家鄉附近。因此鑑三很可能在後來還能回憶起童年最重大事件所伴隨的那種不確定感。正如同在美國二十世紀二〇年代出生的一代被稱為「大蕭條之子」，同樣也可以說鑑三成長為一個「維新之子」。

他的家族成員是武士；這個階級在社會中地位最高。維新之後發生的事件終結了武士的統治，內村家和其他類似的家族因此衰落。武士階級只佔人口的百分之五左右，其形成基礎是軍事武力。經過歷代相傳，武士逐漸除了防禦職責外，還被委以民政行政和世俗學問的功能。全國由二百多個半自治的政治單位（藩）加上最高權力的皇室制度組成，每個武士相對於其藩主——他所在藩的統治者——都有各自的角色。總體而言，每個武士在行使這一角色時，都意識到自己的身分、能力和責任。
維新後的八年間，隨著新制度取代舊社會的舊體制，武士階層逐漸喪失了其功能。隨著目的的消失，他們也失去了政府的俸祿。最有才能的武士轉而進入新社會的各個職位，他們優越的訓練和經驗使他們能夠勝任任何機遇。但也有人無法適應；相反地，他們緊抓著舊秩序的破碎殘片，似乎仍然寄望著對一種已然過時的生活方式的忠誠能換來某種報償。鑑三的父親正屬於這第二類人。
內村鑑三的家人——他的父母、兄弟姊妹以及更遠的親戚——教導他如何作為一個人對待他人時的行為與反應。就在外國幹預的威脅所帶來的變化開始在他家這個小世界裡造成混亂之際，鑑三學會了這些技能。

或許鑑三世界最重要的特徵，就是那些男人似乎不像男人那樣行動；他們無法提供那種讓妻兒感到安心放心的支持。鑑三的父系祖父與家人同住，直到鑑三四歲時去世。他記得祖父是武士刻板印象的化身，在一個已不再需要他的世界裡作為軍人毫無作為。「他最高興的時刻，就是穿著笨重的甲冑現身，佩帶著竹弓、雉羽箭和五十磅重的火槍。」鑑三的外公在鑑三出生前二十年就去世了，似乎當時還是年輕人。成人後，內村記述他的外公「本質上是誠實的人」，因為當被迫接受領主的貸款時，他親自從口袋裡掏錢還清高額利息。在這樣的情況下，許多武士強迫他們部下的人接受小額貸款，利率卻更高。內村自豪地指出他兩位祖父的誠實以及完全戒酒。但日漸的貧困籠罩著鑑三的童年，對一個男孩來說，這些特徵與其說反映了做正確事情的關懷，不如說暗示了缺乏男子氣概。

少年鑑三和成人內村都無法輕易給父親義行定性。在自傳式著作《我如何成為基督徒》中，內村深情地憶及義行作為學者和導師的才能，但其他文獻則表明，隨著鑑三漸長，他認為父親效能不彰。雖然當鑑三還是青少年時義行顯得軟弱，但作為青年的他曾表現出相當的才華。內村家在武士階級中的身分是馬廻役；這一身分帶有微薄的世襲俸祿，使家族能夠過著舒適但非奢華的生活。我們對義行父親才能的了解表明，這筆雖以慣例固定的俸祿，與他對社會的實際貢獻是相稱的。義行本人早期的職業記錄反映了更高的能力。除其他外，他懂得軍事事務，並曾早年建議將其藩的軍隊現代化。世襲身分制度保有足夠的彈性，使一位有才幹的人可以在行政結構中升至高於其傳統家族身分的地位。在鑑三出生之際，義行年約三十歲；他似乎當時在其大名的服下充任一種私人秘書的角色，駐在首都江戶，後來成為東京。各個藩在許多方面是日本世界內的自治邦國，在江戶都保有辦事處。它們在與中央政府的談判中起著大使館的作用，而江戶辦事處附屬的人員代表其藩中較有才能的分子。鑑三的大名——高崎藩的大西照成，該藩位於江戶西方山麓——對年長的內村推崇備至。

鑑三五歲時，吉行獲得四項新的職位；每項職位的名銜都暗示著相當的責任。這種升遷並未持續太久。七個月內，他便被解除職務，被派回藩內的一個小城市。在那裡，他從事的工作重要性低得多。不清楚究竟發生了什麼事，但這次異動似乎源於吉行建議該藩軍隊進行西化。這樣的建議勢必引起其他武士的強烈反對，因為他們的身分讓他們在舊體制中有既得利益。無論如何，全家從繁華的全國政治中心遷移到寧靜的地方城市。他們在那裡度過了隱居般的生活，直到維新後不久。

然後，命運再次眷顧。在維新初期的混亂中，新政府與原有的大名分享政治責任。作為妥協的一部分，中央政府選任最高長官，而原有的大名則選擇次級官員。大河內照仁將吉行從半退休狀態召喚出來，任命他為這些助理官員之一，負責高崎曾被分配但未曾傳統統治過的地區。這是大河內所能賜予的最高職位。在接下來的幾年裡，吉行經歷了數次變動。每次他都晉升到曾由更高階官員擔任的職位。他可能按照習俗，改了名字以應時運。全家隨之遷移。內村家從東京西邊的高崎遷至東京北方遙遠的石卷，這次搬遷在鑑三心中留下了美好的回憶。行程耗時十二天。一家五口乘坐著轎子，每頂轎子配有三名抬夫，此外還有他父親的僕人和年幼的助手，因此是「規模相當可觀的隊伍」。鑑三記得在途中他們通過身子探出轎子，採摘沿路生長的栗子吃。對一個小學男生來說，那是多麼難忘的旅程！

鑑三的父親曾經有一段時間完全掌管一個藩。這是他職業生涯的高峰。多年之後，內村回顧往事，感歎由於父親當時擔任藩知事，「若一切順利」，他至少應該在明治政府數年後建立的新式西方貴族制中成為男爵。然而這並未發生。吉行還未能真正在這個職位上站穩腳跟，大老中·大給恆就將他召回了。吉行出於個人的忠誠而回返，雖然他本可以留在原地。他在高崎的職位名稱保持不變，但新的職責並未給予他展現才能的同樣機會。不久之後，中央政府撤回了大給的臨時權力，結果是吉行幾乎無事可做。他再次被調往一個遠低於前職的位置。1872年，他被迫退職；此時他才剛過四十歲，官僚生涯就此結束。鑑三當時十一歲。吉行試圖務農一陣子，隨後用遺留的退職金在東京（曾名江戶）買了一所房子。在鑑三二十多歲的七年間，吉行在大給位於東京的家宅服侍，但除此之外，他幾乎沒有為家庭做過什麼貢獻。他留在家中，「讀書、作詩、下圍棋」，直到在鑑三的影響下成為基督徒之前，他還「喝酒」。
